title: In Defense of Masochism
html:
A friend memed something I said during a philosophical discussion:

I stand by that.

We like feeling good, by definition. And whether or not we’re aware of it, we spend most of our lives in a continual effort to move away from bad feelings and toward good ones. 

We prefer the silky blanket over the scratchy one, the yellow banana over the green one (unless you’re a psychopath), and the beautiful painting over the ugly one. This is why I said everybody is a hedonist: We are all, at bottom, pleasure seekers.

But feeling good isn’t as straightforward as we might hope. Many of life’s deepest pleasures depend on knowledge, physical health, and/or human connection. So, these experiences are, in a sense, paywalled. And for better or for worse, pain is the currency with which we must pay for them.

You want to be smart?

Great. Learning is painful.

You want to be fit?

Great. Exercise is painful.

You want to be loved?

Great. Being vulnerable is painful.

Good hedonists turn towards pain and pay upfront, putting pain before pleasure (think good workouts, hard study sessions, honesty, etc). They’re compensated in turn with durable states of well-being. 

Bad hedonists seek their pleasure first (think drugs, alcohol, hookers, etc). They forget, however, that pleasure and pain are forever in a balancing act. In exchange for their pleasure, they pay with hangovers, withdrawals, and regret. 

So yeah… Everybody is a hedonist. Some people just suck at it. 

But where do we go from here? Who can we look to for guidance on how to be a good hedonist?

Masochists? Maybe 🤷. 

Our immersion in the pleasure-pain duality may offer some credence to the masochists. If pain is a prerequisite to reliable states of well-being, should we not aim to enjoy it? 

We know it’s possible. Many of us know the strangely satisfying burn in your legs that arises amidst a hard set of squats or a long run. We’ve been conditioned to enjoy this pain because we know it’s a good omen. We know what’s on the other side of the discomfort, so we can sit in it and, at times, relish it. Through accepting and even enjoying pain, we can find pleasure in the valleys of life, as well as the peaks.

“Pain makes me grow. Growing is what I want. Therefore, for me pain is pleasure.” – Arnold Schwarzenegger

So, do hard things, put pain first, and when the going gets tough, remember what former Navy SEAL Jocko Wilink would say – “Good”.

Happy hedoning.
